title: Booking.com Search Rows Hide 9–16% of the Price in a Field Labelled 21, 22 and 23
author: Nikita Iakovlev
summary: I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into scrapers on Apify, and one of them reads Booking.com search pages: destination in, one row per property out, with the price for your dates, the matched room, the rating and the location. The field people build their spreadsheet on is priceTotal . It is the number Booking prints in the search card, it is the number the site sorts by, and it is not the number anybody pays. On 12 October 2026 I ran the same stay — 20 to 23 November 2026, two adults, one room — against four destinations and read all 24 rows. Here is what the excluded-charges field said. 24 rows, four cities, nothing tax-inclusive Destination priceTotal range Excluded charges Share of the headline price Lisbon (EUR) €289.81 – €540.27 flat €24 + 6.00% 10.4% – 14.3% New York (USD) $370.15 – $1438.51 flat $10.50 + 14.75% 0% – 16.2% Tokyo (USD) $483.42 – $1101.10 9.01% – 10.00% 9.0% – 10.0% Bali (USD) $96.09 – $875.27 9.01% or 10.99% 9.0% – 11.0% Read the New York column slowly. priceTotal for the Hyatt Regency Times Square was $1120.95, and the row also carried $175.84 of charges that price does not contain. The guest pays $1296.79. If your rate-shopping table says $1120.95, your table is wrong by the size of a whole night. Two of the per-city numbers are suspiciously exact, and that is the useful part: New York: 14.75%, to the cent, on every row that had it. $110.06 on $746.20. $138.15 on $936.63. $212.18 on $1438.51. A percentage that stable is a tax rate, not an estimate. Lisbon: a flat €24 on all six properties , regardless of a price range that runs from €290 to €540. Three nights, two guests, €24 — €4 per guest per night, charged per stay rather than per euro spent. Tokyo came back at 10.00% on five rows and 9.01% on one. Bali is the interesting one: within a single destination, three properties excluded 9.01% and three excluded 10.99%, and which rate applied tracked exactly with the charge code in the field. The field has amounts but no names This is what taxesAndFeesExcluded actually looks like: { "name" : "Hyatt Regency Times Square" , "priceTotal" : 1120.95 , "currency" : "USD" , "taxesAndFeesExcluded" : [ "22: $10.50" , "23: $165.34" ], "taxesAndFeesExcludedTotal" : 175.8402 , "chargesInfo" : null } 22 and 23 are not my invention and not a truncation. Booking's GraphQL search response returns excluded charges as a list of objects carrying chargeMode , chargeInclusion , chargeType and amountPerStay — and for an anonymous caller chargeType is an integer. There is no translation node next to it, the way there is on badges, cancellation copy and review text. The site renders "+ taxes and charges" and hides the breakdown behind a tooltip that is assembled elsewhere. My first version of this mapper expected names and produced "CITYTAX: US$18.24" in a code comment that never matched reality. The field was empty on every row for a while, because I was reading a translation key that is not there. Across the four markets the codes behaved consistently enough to describe, though not enough to label: 22 was always a flat amount per stay, identical across every property in a city: €24 in Lisbon, $10.50 in New York, $0 in Tokyo and on three Bali rows. 21 and 23 were always a percentage of priceTotal : 6% in Lisbon, 14.75% in New York, 10% in Tokyo, 9.01% under code 21 and 10.99% under code 23 in Bali. I ship the integers. I am not going to guess that 22 means "city tax" and put a word in a dataset column on the strength of six rows per market, because the moment I do, someone builds a VAT reclaim report on it. An unexplained 22 makes you go look. A wrong CITYTAX does not. What it does to a sorted table The percentage is near-constant inside a city, so within-city ranking mostly survives. I checked all 24 rows: adding the excluded charges did not flip a single pair. Lisbon stayed in the same order; New York stayed in the same order. Cross-city comparison is where it breaks. A $500 Tokyo stay really costs about $550. A $500 New York stay really costs about $580. Build a "cheapest city for a three-night trip" chart on priceTotal and you have quietly handed New York a 6% discount it does not get. So compute the honest number before you sort: import requests rows = requests . post ( " https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~booking-hotels-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items " , params = { " token " : TOKEN }, json = { " mode " : " search " , " destination " : " New York " , " checkin " : " 2026-11-20 " , " checkout " : " 2026-11-23 " , " adults " : 2 , " currency " : " USD " , " sortBy " : " price " , " maxResults " : 25 , }, ). json () for r in sorted ( rows , key = lambda r : r [ " priceTotal " ] + ( r . get ( " taxesAndFeesExcludedTotal " ) or 0 )): true_total = r [ " priceTotal " ] + ( r . get ( " taxesAndFeesExcludedTotal " ) or 0 ) print ( f ' { r [ " name " ][ : 40 ] : 40 } { r [ " priceTotal " ] : 8.2 f } -> { true_total : 8.2 f } ' ) Note the or 0 . Which brings me to the bug this article found in my own code. The zero that looked like a missing value West Side YMCA, cheapest row in the New York sort at $370.15, came back like this: { "taxesAndFeesExcluded" : [ "23: $0" ], "taxesAndFeesExcludedTotal" : null } ["23: $0"] is real: Booking returns the charge line with an amount of zero. But my aggregate was null , because the mapper ended in || null — and in JavaScript 0 || null is null . A property with genuinely no extra charges was indistinguishable from a property whose charges I failed to read. On a 25-row New York search, two rows were affected: West Side YMCA and HI New York City Hostel, both hostel-style properties. One character, || to ?? , except I removed the fallback entirely since the coercion already yields null for a missing field. Fixed and live as build 0.1.33 today; those two rows now report 0 . If you pulled this Actor's data before 12 October 2026 and treated taxesAndFeesExcludedTotal: null as "unknown, skip the row", you dropped the cheapest properties in the market. The other half of the row is prose, not data While confirming the tax numbers I changed the language input and watched the same property come back four ways. MASA Hotel & Spa, Lisbon, same dates: language distanceFromCentre en-us (default) 2.6 miles from downtown en-gb 2.6 miles from centre de Zentrum: 4,2 km fr 4,2 km du centre Three things worth knowing before you parse that column: It is a sentence, not a number. There is no numeric distance field in the search response — Booking sends location.mainDistance already rendered. English means imperial, even British English. en-gb changed "downtown" to "centre" and left the miles alone. Metric arrives only when you leave English, and then with a comma decimal separator: 4,2 km . The wording changes, so your regex is locale-bound. de puts the label first and a colon in the middle. Use latitude and longitude instead and compute the distance yourself. They are plain floats and they do not translate. The same split hits reviewScoreWord : Wonderful in English, Sehr gut in German, Très bien in French. Filter on that string and your pipeline silently empties the day someone sets a language. Filter on reviewScore , which stays 9.3 . What does not translate is the half of the row my own code assembles: propertyType and roomBeds stayed Hotel and 1 king bed under de and fr , because those come from integer→name tables inside the Actor, not from Booking. So a non-English run gives you a row that is half localised and half English, and the seam runs exactly along "who mapped this field". Worth knowing if you ever diff two runs and wonder why only some columns moved. One more locale trap: priceTotalText is a formatted string — "$147.25" but "€ 524.51" , with a non-breaking space and the symbol on the other side. Parse priceTotal , which is a float. Region searches have no centre Bali returned destinationType: "REGION" and distanceFromCentre: null on all six rows. Lisbon, New York and Tokyo came back as "CITY" and filled it on every row. That is not a failure — a 5,780 km² island does not have a downtown — but if your dashboard has a "distance from centre" axis, it will be empty for every region, landmark and country-level search you run. Check destinationType before you plot it. When this is the wrong tool You need to actually book. This reads public search data. Taking a reservation means Booking's affiliate programme, which is a contract, not a scraper. You need yesterday's prices. Nothing stores the past. Hotel pricing is only observable going forward, so schedule a daily run now if you want a history in March. You need the exact final figure at checkout. The excluded charges are Booking's own estimate of what the property will add; resort fees, card fees and local levies collected at the desk are not all in there. You need every rate of 500 hotels. Rooms and rates mean a request per property. That is fine for fifty and slow for five hundred. If reading hotel search data as rows is what you want, the Actor is Booking.com Hotel Search Scraper — search, single hotel, reviews and a year-ahead price calendar, no browser and no login. The four-city measurement in this post cost 7 cents. And whatever you use to get the data: before you sort by price, add the field that says the price is incomplete.

title: The Camera-Trap Data Standard Starts With When the Camera Was Running, Not What It Saw
author: Super Funicular
summary: Three raccoon visits in a week reads like a fact about raccoons. It is at least as much a fact about the camera: how many of those nights it was running, how far out it could make out movement, and whether the clock stamping each clip was right. Wildlife researchers who leave cameras out unattended share a data format that makes them write those things down, and it gives them a table of their own, ahead of anything the camera saw. The format is Camtrap DP, maintained by the Camtrap DP Development Team under Biodiversity Information Standards (TDWG). I read its data specification and its FAQ for this piece. I build a camera app for old Android phones and I am not an ecologist, so nothing here is a survey method. What the standard offers a person with a phone pointed at a yard, a feeder or the gap under a fence is a checklist: what to record so that a count can later be read as a rate. Three tables, and the first one describes the camera The specification opens its data section plainly: "Data in Camtrap DP are organized as three related resources (CSV files): deployments , media and observations ." Media is the files. Observations are what a person, or a model, decided was in them. Deployments are the camera's own record: where it was, how it was set up, and for how long. Every media file and every observation carries a deploymentID that points back to that first table, so nothing the camera recorded can drift loose from the window it was recorded in. Of the required fields in the deployments table, two are about time. The start is defined as "Date and time at which the deployment was started. Formatted as an ISO 8601 string with timezone designator", and the end gets the matching definition. The timezone part deserves a pause. A clip stamped with a bare date and time names a moment only if you know which clock produced it. With a UTC offset attached it names one instant anywhere. A phone that crossed a time zone, or a folder of clips copied to a computer set to a different zone, is how a naive timestamp quietly moves by hours, and nothing in the file announces it. The fields that describe what the camera could see Beyond time, the deployments table has room for the physical setup. Among them: cameraHeight , in meters. cameraTilt , in degrees, from facing straight down to facing straight up. cameraHeading , in degrees clockwise from north. detectionDistance , defined as "Maximum distance at which the camera can reliably detect activity. Expressed in meters. Typically measured by having a human move in front of the camera." That last definition is a procedure, and it is the most useful sentence in the document for anyone mounting a phone. Have someone walk across the frame at increasing distances, then open the recording and find the furthest point at which you can still tell that a body went past. For a phone that records continuously rather than on a trigger, that is my working reading of "detect": the reviewer can see it. Do the walk once in daylight and once after dark, because the answer changes with the light, and write down both. A second field matters if your setup records on motion: cameraDelay , "Predefined duration after detection when further activity is ignored. Expressed in seconds." During that window a lingering animal is one clip and a second animal arriving behind it may be no clip at all. If your setup records continuously, the field stays empty. If it records on motion, the delay is a setting worth finding and writing down, because it shapes every count that follows. Then there is timestampIssues , a flag for deployments whose media timestamps are "known to have (unsolvable) issues (e.g. unknown timezone, am/pm switch)". The standard keeps a place for a clock it cannot repair rather than dropping the data or pretending the clock was fine. That is a good habit on its own: if you are not sure the phone's clock was right, say so next to the data. Gaps belong in the structure, not in a note The deployments table has a start and an end, and I read the full field list for anything describing an interruption inside a deployment. There is a free-text deploymentComments field and nothing structured for downtime. So under this layout, a camera that stopped for a day and a half reads most cleanly as two deployments, not one deployment with a caveat. That is my reading of the schema rather than a rule the spec states, and it is the habit worth borrowing: when the phone was unplugged, the battery ran flat, or someone lifted it down to look at it, close the row, and open a new one when it is running again. This matters because a gap is where false nulls live. A night with no clips is evidence that nothing came only if the camera was running that night. Count empty nights against a calendar and every night the camera was dark gets counted as a night nothing visited. Blanks are observations too The observations table has a required type with six allowed values: "animal, human, vehicle, blank, unknown, unclassified". Blank is a category of its own. A clip set off by wind, a headlight sweep or a moth can be recorded as blank rather than deleted. Keeping blanks earns its space twice. They show the camera was alive at that hour, and their share tells you whether a placement is mostly wind and headlights before you spend evenings reviewing it. The standard also has a cameraSetupType field whose two values are setup and calibration, so the clips of you adjusting the mount are labelled as that instead of being counted as a visitor. Count events, not files The subtlest definition in the spec is observationLevel . Observations at the media level are tied to a single file and are "especially useful for machine learning and don't need to be mutually exclusive (e.g. multiple classifications are allowed)". Observations at the event level cover a group of files and "should be mutually exclusive, so that their count can be summed." The practical version: a raccoon that ambles through over several minutes may land in more than one file, especially if a recorder splits long recordings into segments. Tally sightings per file and that single visit is counted as many times as there are files. Group the files into one event first, then count. The spec defines an event as a collection of media files and, in the fields I read, sets no time rule for how to group them, so pick a rule, write it down, and keep it. A rate needs a denominator Here is the whole idea in a small script. Two files, shaped like the standard's tables with only the columns needed. The first is the deployment log, kept by hand: deploymentID,deploymentStart,deploymentEnd,cameraHeight,cameraTilt,cameraHeading,detectionDistance,timestampIssues,deploymentComments yard-01,2026-10-01T18:00:00-04:00,2026-10-04T07:30:00-04:00,0.5,0,200,6.5,false,phone in fence-post box yard-02,2026-10-05T19:15:00-04:00,2026-10-09T07:00:00-04:00,0.5,0,200,6.5,false,restarted after charger unplugged The second holds event-level observations. Notice that o6 sits in the day and a half between the two deployments: observationID,deploymentID,eventStart,eventEnd,observationLevel,observationType,scientificName,count o1,yard-01,2026-10-01T18:02:10-04:00,2026-10-01T18:02:40-04:00,event,human,,1 o2,yard-01,2026-10-02T02:14:00-04:00,2026-10-02T02:15:30-04:00,event,animal,Procyon lotor,2 o3,yard-01,2026-10-03T23:40:00-04:00,2026-10-03T23:41:00-04:00,event,blank,, o4,yard-02,2026-10-06T01:05:00-04:00,2026-10-06T01:06:00-04:00,event,animal,Procyon lotor,1 o5,yard-02,2026-10-07T21:30:00-04:00,2026-10-07T21:31:00-04:00,event,animal,Vulpes vulpes,1 o6,yard-02,2026-10-04T23:00:00-04:00,2026-10-04T23:01:00-04:00,event,animal,Procyon lotor,1 The script divides animal events by the hours the log says the camera was out, and refuses to quietly count anything that falls outside a logged window. Timestamps without an offset are rejected outright: import csv from collections import Counter from datetime import datetime def ts ( s ): t = datetime . fromisoformat ( s . replace ( ' Z ' , ' +00:00 ' )) assert t . tzinfo is not None , f ' no UTC offset: { s } ' return t deps = {} for r in csv . DictReader ( open ( ' deployments.csv ' )): start , end = ts ( r [ ' deploymentStart ' ]), ts ( r [ ' deploymentEnd ' ]) assert end > start , r [ ' deploymentID ' ] deps [ r [ ' deploymentID ' ]] = ( start , end ) days = sum (( e - s ). total_seconds () for s , e in deps . values ()) / 86400 print ( f ' effort: { days : . 2 f } camera-days over { len ( deps ) } deployments ' ) hits , outside = Counter (), [] for r in csv . DictReader ( open ( ' observations.csv ' )): if r [ ' observationLevel ' ] != ' event ' or r [ ' observationType ' ] != ' animal ' : continue s , e = deps [ r [ ' deploymentID ' ]] if not ( s <= ts ( r [ ' eventStart ' ]) <= e ): outside . append ( r [ ' observationID ' ]) continue hits [ r [ ' scientificName ' ]] += 1 for name , n in hits . most_common (): print ( f ' { name } : { n } events, { 100 * n / days : . 1 f } per 100 camera-days ' ) if outside : print ( ' outside their deployment window: ' , ' , ' . join ( outside )) Run with Python 3.10, it prints: effort: 6.05 camera-days over 2 deployments Procyon lotor: 2 events, 33.0 per 100 camera-days Vulpes vulpes: 1 events, 16.5 per 100 camera-days outside their deployment window: o6 Two things in that output are worth more than the rates themselves. First, the rate uses 6.05 camera-days, not the calendar span. The same records counted from the first start to the last end cover 7.54 days, and dividing the two raccoon events by that gives 26.5 per 100 instead of 33.0, because 1.49 of those days had no camera watching. The calendar version is wrong in the comfortable direction: it makes a place look quieter than it is. Second, o6 is reported, not counted. The log says the camera was off, and a record says it was on. One of the two is wrong: either the restart went unlogged, or the clip carries a bad timestamp, which is exactly what timestampIssues exists to flag. The script cannot tell which, and it should not guess. Counting it would lift the raccoon rate to 39.8 per 100 calendar days, with nothing in the output to show where the extra visit came from. The count column holds individuals per event, and the script ignores it on purpose. Two raccoons in one clip is one visit; summing individuals answers a different question, and mixing the two inside one number is how a tally inflates. Small numbers deserve a plain warning. Three events over six days is an anecdote with a unit attached. The unit is still the point: it is what lets you compare this month with next month, or the fence post with the shed, as long as both denominators are written down. Move the phone, change its height or heading, and that is a new deployment, since a rate from one setup says little about another. What I did not establish Whether rates from a phone camera can be compared with rates from a dedicated trail camera. Lens, trigger and night illumination all differ, and I have no data on how much that moves a count. How researchers in a given study define an independent event. The standard leaves room for the rule; it does not supply one in the fields I read. How any particular app names, splits or timestamps its files. I am describing a published data standard and a short script, not the internals of my own product or anyone else's. Which version of the specification a future reader will see. title: llms.txt: what it is, how to write one, and whether it actually does anything
author: Mayank Sharma
summary: Every few months a new file shows up that promises to make your site "AI-ready". The current one is llms.txt . We publish one on our own site, and I've read the arguments on both sides, so here is what I'd tell a developer who just got a ticket that says "add llms.txt". Short version: it's cheap to add and harmless, it's useful for coding assistants and docs, and there's no public evidence yet that it changes whether ChatGPT or Perplexity cite you. Ship it if it takes ten minutes; don't sell it to your boss as an SEO win. What llms.txt is llms.txt is a proposal published at llmstxt.org in September 2024 by Jeremy Howard of Answer.AI. The idea: put a Markdown file at the root of your site ( https://example.com/llms.txt ) that gives a language model a short, curated map of your most useful pages. Why not just use sitemap.xml ? A sitemap lists every URL for a crawler. llms.txt is meant to be read by a model at inference time, with limited context, so it's short, human-written and annotated. Think "README for your website", not "index of everything". The format The spec is small. In order: An H1 with the name of the site or project. This is the only required part. A blockquote with a one-paragraph summary. Optional free text with anything a model should know. H2 sections, each with a Markdown list of links: - [Title](url): short note . An optional section literally called ## Optional for links that can be skipped when context is tight. Here's a realistic example for a small SaaS: # Acme Invoices > Acme Invoices is invoicing software for freelancers in the EU. It creates > VAT-compliant invoices, tracks payments and exports to accounting tools. Prices are in EUR. There is a free plan for up to 5 invoices a month. ## Product - [ Features ]( https://acme.example/features ) : What the app does, with screenshots - [ Pricing ]( https://acme.example/pricing ) : Plans, limits and what's in the free tier ## Docs - [ Getting started ]( https://acme.example/docs/start ) : Create your first invoice - [ API reference ]( https://acme.example/docs/api ) : REST endpoints and auth ## Optional - [ Changelog ]( https://acme.example/changelog ) : Release notes A few things that make the difference between a useful file and noise: Write the notes yourself. "Plans, limits and what's in the free tier" helps a model choose a link. A copied meta description usually doesn't. Leave things out. Thank-you pages, login, tag archives and thin pages don't belong there. Short is the point. Keep it current. A link to a page that 404s is worse than no link. The proposal also suggests offering clean Markdown versions of pages (for example /docs/start.md ) and an llms-full.txt with the full text inlined. Those are optional, and most sites skip them. Shipping it As a static file (any stack) Put llms.txt wherever your framework serves static files from the root: public/ in Next.js, Vite and Create React App, static/ in SvelteKit and Hugo, the web root on a plain server. Check it returns 200 with a text content type: curl -sI https://your-site.com/llms.txt | head -n 5 Generated in Next.js (App Router) If your pages come from a CMS, generate the file so it never drifts out of date: // app/llms.txt/route.ts import { getPublishedPages } from " @/lib/cms " ; export const revalidate = 86400 ; // rebuild daily export async function GET () { const pages = await getPublishedPages (); // [{ title, url, summary, section }] const sections = new Map < string , string [] > (); for ( const p of pages ) { const line = `- [ ${ p . title } ]( ${ p . url } ): ${ p . summary } ` ; sections . set ( p . section , [...( sections . get ( p . section ) ?? []), line ]); } const body = [ " # Acme Invoices " , "" , " > Invoicing software for EU freelancers: VAT-compliant invoices, payment tracking, accounting exports. " , "" , ...[... sections ]. flatMap (([ name , lines ]) => [ `## ${ name } ` , "" , ... lines , "" ]), ]. join ( " \n " ); return new Response ( body , { headers : { " Content-Type " : " text/plain; charset=utf-8 " }, }); } If you'd rather not write one by hand, I work on a free llms.txt generator at Presence Scout. It drafts the file from your sitemap and existing page titles, with no AI-written text, so you get a starting point to edit rather than a finished file. The notes will only be as good as your titles and descriptions, which is honestly true of any generator. Does it actually do anything? This is where I'd be careful. Where it clearly helps: developer tools. Coding assistants and agents work better when you hand them a compact map of a library's docs, and a lot of documentation sites now publish llms.txt for exactly that reason. If you maintain an API or an SDK, this alone justifies the file. Where the evidence is thin: AI search. I haven't seen any of the major assistants document that their crawlers fetch llms.txt and use it to decide what to cite. So treat claims like "llms.txt gets you into ChatGPT answers" as unproven. What matters more for AI search: whether the crawlers can read your pages at all. If robots.txt , your CDN's bot rules or a JavaScript-only render keep them out, no index file will fix it. Check that first; a five-line curl with the crawler's user agent will tell you more than any new file. My checklist [ ] Crawlers can fetch your key pages (status 200, real HTML, not a JS shell) [ ] llms.txt at the root, under ~50 links, with hand-written notes [ ] No links to private, thin or redirecting pages [ ] Generated from your CMS, or on a reminder to review quarterly It's a small file. Treat it like one: quick to ship, easy to maintain, and not a strategy on its own. I'm Mayank, Digital Marketing Manager at Presence Scout. We build tools that show where a brand appears in AI answers and Google results.

title: Passkeys Can Lock You Out of Your Own Device. Here's How.
author: James Anderson
summary: Let me say the reassuring part first, because this is not a "don't use passkeys" piece: passkeys are genuinely good, they're a real upgrade over passwords, and I use them. If you take nothing else from this, take that. But there's a part of how passkeys work that the "add passkey auth in 10 minutes" tutorials never mention, and it's the one part actually worth understanding — because it's the part with teeth. Under the right (or wrong) conditions, the passkey system can let a website verify what device and software you're using and refuse to log you in if it doesn't approve. In principle, that can lock you out of your own account on your own device, for running the "wrong" operating system or browser. That sounds alarming, and the mechanism is real, so I want to explain it honestly — both how it genuinely works and how worried you should actually be, because the answer to the second part is "less than the headline suggests, but not zero." This piece was sparked by a more alarmist article making the rounds ("passkeys are a trap"), and I wanted to write the fair, technical version: what's true, what's overblown, and — if you're the one building auth — the choice that quietly lands on your desk. The feature is called attestation. Here's the whole story. First, how passkeys actually work Quick, because the rest depends on it. A passkey is a public/private key pair, created by your authenticator — your phone, your laptop, or a hardware key like a YubiKey. When you register, the authenticator generates the pair, keeps the private key locked away (ideally in a secure chip it never leaves), and hands the website the public key. To log in, the site sends a challenge, your authenticator signs it with the private key, and the site verifies the signature with the public key it stored. Why this is genuinely better than passwords: there's no shared secret to steal — the site never holds anything that logs you in, so a database breach leaks public keys, which are useless to an attacker. And it's phishing-resistant, because the key is bound to the real domain; a fake look-alike site can't trigger it. This part is great. No notes. The standard underneath is WebAuthn (a W3C/FIDO standard), and "passkey" is just the friendly user-facing name for a WebAuthn credential. So far, so good. "Passkey" is an umbrella, not one thing Here's the first thing the marketing glosses over: "passkey" isn't a single thing. It's a spectrum of options. A passkey can be synced across your devices (the convenient kind, backed up to iCloud or Google) or device-bound (never leaves one piece of hardware). It can live on the device you're using ( platform ) or roam between devices over Bluetooth/NFC ( roaming , like a YubiKey). Most of these distinctions are benign — they're just convenience-vs-control tradeoffs you'd reasonably want either way. But one property is different in kind, because it's not about your convenience at all. It's about what the website gets to know and demand about your setup. That's attestation. What attestation actually is When you register a passkey, the authenticator can include a signed statement that proves what kind of authenticator created the key — its make and model — in a way that can't be faked, because it's signed using a key baked into the device's secure chip at manufacture. That's the core idea: attestation attests to the provenance of the authenticator. Not who you are — what device you used. There are levels of it, and the differences matter: none — the default. No device info, or an anonymized version. The site gets your public key and nothing identifying about your hardware. This is what the overwhelming majority of sites use. direct — the site receives the authenticator's make and model (e.g. "this is a YubiKey 5" or "this is an iOS platform authenticator"). enterprise — the strong one: the attestation can include uniquely identifying information, like a serial number. This is meant for controlled deployments where a company issues a known fleet of keys. And here is the mechanism behind the scary headline: because an attested registration cryptographically proves what device and software stack produced the key, a website can decide to accept only certain ones. "We only accept hardware-backed, user-verified, attested passkeys from approved authenticators." If your setup can't produce that proof — because you're on Linux, or a de-Googled phone, or a custom browser, or an OS that's no longer getting the blessed updates — the site can notice, and refuse you. That's the lock-out. It's real, and that's genuinely how it would work. So how worried should you actually be? (Honestly: watchful, not scared) This is where the alarmist version stops and the honest version has to keep going, because the mechanism being possible is very different from it being likely to hit you today. Here's the real context, and most of it is reassuring. Attestation defaults to none , and the professional consensus is to leave it there. The W3C spec defaults the attestation setting to none , and current (2026) guidance for developers is blunt about it: for almost all consumer and business sign-ins, you should not request attestation. It leaks platform information, reduces user choice, and adds friction for no benefit to a normal login. "Skip it" is the mainstream recommendation, not a fringe one. The identifying kind needs your consent and specific configuration. Enterprise attestation — the type that can include serial numbers — can't just be silently switched on against a consumer. It requires the authenticator to support it, the platform/browser to be configured (typically by enterprise policy) to release it, and user consent. It's a managed-workplace tool, not something a random website can spring on you. Privacy is built into the standard on purpose. To stop attestation from becoming a tracking identifier, FIDO guidance requires each attestation certificate to be shared across at least 100,000 devices in a batch. So "direct" attestation tells a site you're using, say, an iPhone 15 — not which iPhone 15. It identifies a model, not a person, by design. And in practice, essentially no mainstream consumer site requires attestation today. The passkeys you actually use — from Apple, Google, or a password manager — are the benign, non-attested, user-friendly kind. The lock-you-out scenario is a capability sitting in the standard, not a wall you're hitting this week. So the honest calibration: the mechanism is real and worth knowing about , because it's the point where authentication could quietly turn into a lever over what software you're allowed to run — and standards have a way of tightening over time. But it is not a trap that's currently sprung, and "passkeys are dangerous, don't use them" is an overreaction to a capability that today sits almost entirely unused against consumers. Watchful, not scared. The part most articles skip: if you're the developer, this is your choice Here's the angle I most wanted to write, because nearly every passkey piece is aimed at users and this one's aimed at you, the person implementing auth. When you add passkeys to your app, attestation is a setting you choose , and the default — none — is almost certainly the right one. Requesting attestation means you receive platform/device information about your users, you add friction, and you risk excluding people on perfectly legitimate but non-mainstream setups. For a normal product, that's all cost and no benefit. So the practical rule is easy: use none unless you have a specific, genuine regulatory or policy reason not to — a regulated workforce that must use issued hardware keys, a high-assurance fleet, a compliance mandate. Those are real and valid. "It felt more secure" is not one of them. But I'd also frame it as more than a technical default, because it is: the moment you require attestation, you've become the one deciding which devices and software your users are allowed to use to reach their own accounts. That's a real power, and a real responsibility. The lock-out this article's title warns about isn't something passkeys do to people on their own — it's something a developer chooses to impose. Most of the time, you shouldn't. Reach for that lever only when you truly must, and know what you're doing to your users' autonomy when you do. What to actually do As a user: use passkeys. They're a big security upgrade and the versions you'll actually encounter are the friendly kind. Just know the word "attestation" and what it enables, so that if the norms ever shift, you'll recognize what's happening instead of being quietly funneled. And if you want maximum control with passkey-grade security, a hardware key like a YubiKey is self-contained and keeps the authority with you. As a developer: default to attestation: none . Only request more when a real policy requires it. And when you do, remember you're not just tightening security — you're deciding what your users are permitted to run. Choose that deliberately. The takeaway Passkeys aren't a trap, and the title isn't a warning to avoid them — it's a warning to understand them. The lock-out is real as a mechanism and, today, almost entirely theoretical in practice, because the setting that enables it defaults off, needs consent in its strong form, and is deliberately privacy-limited. But it's worth knowing, for one reason that runs deeper than passwords ever did: attestation is the point where "proving who you are" quietly gains the ability to enforce "what you're allowed to run." It's benign now. It's the dial to watch. And if you're the one building the login, it's a dial that's in your hand — so keep it set to "trust the user" unless you have a very good reason not to. Two honest questions. As a user: does knowing about attestation change how you feel about passkeys — or is this a non-issue being blown out of proportion? And as a developer: has anyone here had a genuine, legitimate reason to require attestation beyond none ? I'd like to hear the real use cases from people who've actually shipped it, because they're rarer than the fear implies. Sources & further reading: WebAuthn is a W3C/FIDO Alliance standard (see the W3C Web Authentication spec and MDN's PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptions docs for the attestation conveyance options). The attestation member defaults to none per spec; current developer guidance (e.g. WebAuthn implementation guides, 2026) recommends none for virtually all consumer and B2B sign-ins and reserving direct / enterprise for regulated or managed-fleet cases. FIDO guidance recommends attestation certificates span ≥100,000 devices per batch to preserve privacy, and enterprise attestation requires authenticator support, platform configuration, and user consent. This piece was prompted by a more alarmist article ("Passkeys are a trap"); I've aimed to present the mechanism accurately and the risk proportionately — verify specifics against the primary WebAuthn spec, which is the authority here.

title: Full feed coverage is not snapshot readiness: a tested JavaScript contract
author: Ali Gürtuna | AGProLabs
summary: A dashboard can display every expected feed and still be unready for comparison. The distinction becomes visible when one source is developing, or when a cached observation belongs to the wrong completed interval. A 4/4 badge answers a coverage question. It cannot establish that four observations satisfy the snapshot policy. Declare the required slots first This example uses two fictional instruments and two timeframes. Each required slot has a symbol, a timeframe and an expected completed close time. A caller provides that plan. The evaluator does not infer exchange sessions or decide which candle should be complete. Daily and four-hour observations need not have equal close timestamps. They need to match their respective expected slots in the same declared plan. Comparing all timestamps for equality would reject legitimate multi-timeframe snapshots. const daily = Date . parse ( " 2026-10-11T00:00:00Z " ); const fourHour = Date . parse ( " 2026-10-11T20:00:00Z " ); const plan = [ " VENUE:A " , " VENUE:B " ]. flatMap ( symbol => [ { symbol , timeframe : " D " , expectedClose : daily }, { symbol , timeframe : " 4H " , expectedClose : fourHour } ]); These timestamps are synthetic fixtures, not an exchange calendar or live market observation. Keep coverage, confirmation and alignment separate The evaluator returns a reason along with the state. An unrelated row cannot replace a missing required slot, and a duplicate cannot increase coverage. Strict boolean confirmation avoids accepting a truthy string such as "false" . // Educational contract, synthetic inputs; not a production trading engine. function assessSnapshot ( plan , rows ) { const waiting = reason => ({ state : ' WAIT ' , reason }); const key = x => JSON . stringify ([ x . symbol , x . timeframe ]); const validKey = x => x && typeof x . symbol === ' string ' && x . symbol . trim () && typeof x . timeframe === ' string ' && x . timeframe . trim (); const validClose = x => Number . isSafeInteger ( x ) && x >= 0 ; if ( ! Array . isArray ( plan ) || ! plan . length || ! Array . isArray ( rows )) { return waiting ( ' INVALID_CONTRACT ' ); } const expected = new Map (); for ( const slot of plan ) { if ( ! validKey ( slot ) || ! validClose ( slot . expectedClose ) || expected . has ( key ( slot ))) { return waiting ( ' INVALID_CONTRACT ' ); } expected . set ( key ( slot ), slot . expectedClose ); } const observed = new Map (); for ( const row of rows ) { if ( ! validKey ( row )) return waiting ( ' INVALID_ROW ' ); const id = key ( row ); if ( ! expected . has ( id )) continue ; // unrelated data does not fill required slots if ( observed . has ( id )) return waiting ( ' DUPLICATE_SLOT ' ); observed . set ( id , row ); } const coverage = { present : observed . size , required : expected . size }; if ( observed . size !== expected . size ) return { ... waiting ( ' INCOMPLETE_COVERAGE ' ), coverage }; for ( const row of observed . values ()) { if ( row . confirmed !== true ) return { ... waiting ( ' UNCONFIRMED_SOURCE ' ), coverage }; } for ( const [ id , row ] of observed ) { if ( ! validClose ( row . closeTime )) return { ... waiting ( ' INVALID_CLOSE_TIME ' ), coverage }; if ( row . closeTime !== expected . get ( id )) { return { ... waiting ( ' SNAPSHOT_MISMATCH ' ), coverage }; } } return { state : ' REVIEW_READY ' , reason : ' CONTRACT_MET ' , coverage }; } The order of checks is deliberate: validate the contract and identities; establish required coverage; check confirmation; then compare completed close slots. Only after those checks does the example produce REVIEW_READY . That label means the illustrative data contract passed. It does not mean a trading candidate qualified. Reproduce the full-coverage failure const rows = plan . map ( p => ({ symbol : p . symbol , timeframe : p . timeframe , closeTime : p . expectedClose , confirmed : true })); // One row belongs to an earlier four-hour slot. rows [ 3 ]. closeTime -= 4 * 3600000 ; console . log ( assessSnapshot ( plan , rows )); // { state: "WAIT", reason: "SNAPSHOT_MISMATCH", // coverage: { present: 4, required: 4 } } This is a useful UI boundary: keep the coverage badge and show the waiting reason beside it. Do not recolor the whole panel as ready merely because the count reached four. Tests that exercise the boundary 13 local contract tests were run , including: distinct Daily/4H close times satisfying one plan; full coverage with a mismatched completed interval; unconfirmed data and the string "true" instead of a boolean; missing slots, duplicate observations and unrelated instruments; empty plans, duplicated expected slots, invalid close values and null rows; preservation of the input arrays. All 13 passed for this small JavaScript function. That result does not validate an actual market feed, a paid indicator, exchange-session scheduling or browser performance. Boundaries worth keeping explicit The upstream producer must establish correct session calendars and expected closes. The row identity uses exact supplied identifiers; it does not normalize symbol aliases or resolve continuous-futures adjustments. Unknown extra instruments are ignored, but a malformed row fails explicitly. The returned reason is the first blocker encountered in the check sequence; a production diagnostic view may need a complete issue list. This example has no price ranking, persistence threshold, liquidity model or order execution. A production system needs its own domain-specific gates, source provenance and failure handling. Where the design question came from The creator-owned Smart Swap and HOLD guide shows a real historical panel with complete coverage and pending time alignment. The confirmation-timing guide explains the separate clocks of chart and higher-timeframe sources. Both are useful interface examples; this function is an independent teaching exercise, not their internal implementation. Disclosure: Trading Suite is an AGProLabs product. This article and illustrative code were prepared by an AI agent for AGProLabs; the contract was checked and the listed local tests were executed during preparation. These are creator-owned project references, not an independent review. The example is analytical education, not financial advice or a promise of results.

title: How to Remove Hum and Buzz From Audio (50Hz vs 60Hz Explained)
author: jacak
summary: Originally published at https://noisewipe.com/blog/remove-hum-and-buzz-from-audio You finish a recording, play it back, and there it is: a low, steady drone sitting under every word. Sometimes it is a soft hum you only notice in the pauses. Sometimes it is a harsh, nasal buzz that makes the whole take sound cheap. Both usually come from the same place: the electricity running through the walls, the cables, and the gear around your microphone. The good news is that this kind of noise is very predictable, which makes it one of the easier problems to fix, both while recording and after the fact. This guide explains where hum and buzz come from, why the 50Hz vs 60Hz difference matters, how to stop it at the source, and how to remove hum from audio online when the recording is already done. It also covers what cleanup can't fix, so you know what to expect. What Hum and Buzz Actually Are Mains electricity is alternating current. It changes direction many times per second, and that rate is called the mains frequency (or utility frequency). When some of that electrical energy leaks into your audio path, you hear it as a tone at that frequency. 50Hz vs 60Hz: it depends on where you record There are two mains frequencies in use around the world: 60Hz in the United States, Canada, Mexico, Brazil, and much of the rest of the Americas, plus a few places in Asia such as South Korea and Saudi Arabia. 50Hz across most of the rest of the world, including Europe, the UK, China, India, Australia, and Africa, and some South American countries such as Argentina and Chile. Japan uses both. Eastern Japan, including Tokyo, runs at 50Hz, while western Japan, including Osaka and Nagoya, runs at 60Hz. So a recording made in London hums at a slightly lower pitch than one made in New York. That matters when you fix it by hand, because you need to target the right frequency. Hum vs buzz Hum is a low, smooth drone at the mains frequency itself, 50Hz or 60Hz. It is often caused by a ground loop. Buzz is harsher and more nasal. It usually sits at double the mains frequency (100Hz or 120Hz) with more tones stacked above it, called harmonics. It typically comes from power supplies or light dimmers. In practice, real recordings often contain the base tone plus a whole series of harmonics, which is why a single cut at 50Hz or 60Hz rarely makes the noise disappear. Common Causes of Hum and Buzz Ground loops. When two pieces of connected gear, such as a computer and an audio interface or mixer, are plugged into different outlets, small voltage differences between their grounds can push current through the audio cable's shield. That current becomes hum. Unbalanced cables. Guitar cables and RCA leads have no built-in noise rejection, so they pick up interference, especially over long runs or when laid next to power cords. Laptop chargers. Many people hear hum appear the moment they plug a laptop in and disappear when it runs on battery. Some chargers also add their own whine. Dimmer switches. Traditional dimmers chop up the mains waveform to lower the brightness, and that chopping radiates buzz into nearby cables. If the buzz stops when the lights go off, you have found the culprit. Air conditioners, fridges, and fans. These add a mix of mechanical rumble and electrical hum from their motors, which is why AC noise in a video often sounds like a hum and a hiss at the same time. Fluorescent lights and cheap power strips. Both are common sources of buzz in home studios and offices. How to Stop Hum While Recording Fixing hum at the source always beats fixing it later. Before your next session, try these: Unplug one thing at a time. Record a few seconds of silence, then disconnect devices one by one until the hum stops. That tells you which connection to fix. Run the laptop on battery. If the hum disappears when the charger is out, record on battery or plug everything into the same outlet or power strip. Use balanced cables. XLR and TRS balanced connections are designed to cancel interference picked up along the cable. Keep cable runs short where you can. Keep audio cables away from power cables. If they have to cross, cross them at a right angle instead of running them side by side. Turn off dimmers and fluorescent lights in the room, or switch them to full brightness, while you record. Use a ground lift or isolation transformer on a DI box or interface if your gear has one. Never remove the ground pin from a power plug. It is unsafe, and audio equipment manufacturers warn against it. Switch off the AC for the few minutes you need a clean take. How to Remove Hum From a Finished Recording If the recording is already done, there are two main approaches. Option 1: Notch filters and EQ Because hum sits at known frequencies, you can cut those frequencies with very narrow notch filters. In Audacity, for example, the Notch Filter effect lets you set a frequency and a width. Find out whether your hum is at 50Hz or 60Hz. A spectrum view in your editor will show a tall peak. Apply a narrow notch at that frequency. Repeat for the harmonics: 100Hz, 150Hz, 200Hz for 50Hz hum, or 120Hz, 180Hz, 240Hz for 60Hz hum. Add a gentle high-pass filter below the lowest part of the voice if rumble remains. This works well when the hum is a clean, steady tone. The downsides are that it takes time, every notch also removes a slice of the voice, and it does nothing for hiss, fans, or other broadband noise mixed in with the hum. Many editors also offer dedicated hum removal plugins that automate the harmonic notches, which is a good choice if you already work in one. Option 2: AI cleanup in your browser with NoiseWipe If you would rather not hunt for frequencies, an AI speech enhancement tool can treat hum, buzz, and hiss together. NoiseWipe runs in your browser, so there is nothing to install. Open the background noise removal page and drop in your file. NoiseWipe accepts MP3, WAV, and M4A audio, plus MP4, MOV, WebM, and MKV video, so you can remove AC noise from video without separating the audio first. Wait for processing. The audio is cleaned with an AI speech enhancement model (DeepFilterNet) that keeps speech and suppresses what isn't speech, whatever its frequency. Listen to the free 30-second cleaned preview. No signup is needed. Pick the section where the hum is loudest and use headphones, because low hum is easy to miss on laptop speakers. If it sounds right, download the full file. Downloads start at $0.99 per file, with hour packs and subscriptions if you clean recordings regularly. The same workflow covers hiss, so if you came here to remove hiss from audio online, the steps are identical. What Cleanup Can and Can't Fix Hum is one of the friendlier kinds of noise, but there are honest limits. Usually fixable Steady mains hum at 50Hz or 60Hz under speech. Buzz and harmonics from chargers, dimmers, and power supplies, as long as the voice is still clearly audible. AC and fan noise mixed with electrical hum. Hiss from high gain or a quiet source. Hard or not fixable Hum louder than the voice. If the drone completely covers parts of the speech, there is not enough voice left to recover. Music recordings. NoiseWipe is built for speech. On a song or an instrument recording, it may treat the music itself as noise, so a careful notch filter is the safer option there. Crackle and distortion. Intermittent pops from a faulty cable or a clipped signal are damage to the waveform, not steady noise, and cleanup won't restore them. The 30-second preview is the quickest way to find out which group your recording falls into before you pay anything. Related guides How to remove background noise from a Zoom recording How to remove background noise from a Voice Memo on iPhone How to remove wind noise from GoPro video FAQ How do I remove hum from audio online? Upload the file to a browser-based tool such as NoiseWipe , listen to the cleaned 30-second preview, and download the full file if it sounds right. There is no software to install and no need to find the hum frequency yourself. Is my hum 50Hz or 60Hz? It depends on where it was recorded. Most of the Americas use 60Hz, while Europe, most of Asia, Africa, and Australia use 50Hz. Japan uses 50Hz in the east and 60Hz in the west. A spectrum view in any audio editor will show the peak. Why does a notch filter at 50Hz or 60Hz not remove all the hum? Hum usually includes harmonics at multiples of the mains frequency, such as 100Hz and 150Hz, or 120Hz and 180Hz. Buzz in particular is strongest at double the mains frequency. You need to notch each harmonic, or use a tool that removes the noise as a whole.
