summary: Long time since an update here - I've been kept busy by various personal things, so involvement on this project has been lower than usual, but I should be getting more towards normal now. While I've done a few other things for the db engine, the binary row representation is the most relevant. Binary rows Basically as said in previous posts, a data page will store a row/record as a contiguous chunk of bytes. Since the rows are variable length, we need to have an encoding for them as well. At its core, the format is compact and pretty clearly organized. We start with a header of course, then we have all the integers (fixed size), then a null bitmap then the string section (which will be variable length). Well, the integer section will be variable as well, depending on the number of integers, but at least we can easily split that one up. The overall layout is: | header | integers | NULL bitmap | string end offsets | string bytes | 6 bytes 4 * I 8 bytes 2 * S B bytes Here: I is the number of integer columns S is the number of string columns B is the total number of UTF-8 bytes used by all string values Header The header itself is 6 bytes long and contains three u16 values: total row size integer column count string column count So the total row size works out to 6 + 4 * I + 8 + 2 * S + B . Integer storage Integer columns are stored in schema order, starting immediately after the header. The first integer starts at byte offset 6 , and integer j starts at 6 + 4 * j . A NULL integer still occupies four bytes and is represented with zero in the payload; the bitmap tells us whether that value is actually NULL or just the integer zero. NULL bitmap The NULL bitmap is a fixed u64 value stored right after the integers. Bit 0 represents the first column, bit 1 the second, and so on. A set bit means NULL. The fixed-size bitmap is a design choice: it handles up to 64 columns, which is enough for now, and any unused bits stay zero. This is the first time I am implementing this concept - the Java version did not support NULL - so idk, things might have implementation wise. Though it was fun to do some bit shifting. Strings and offsets Strings are stored after the bitmap as a sequence of end offsets and then the UTF-8 payload itself. Each string column means one u16 in the end offset array. These offsets are relative to the beginning of the string-data section, not to the row itself. To find string j , we look at its end offset and the previous string end offset. The first string starts at offset 0 . This means if the end offsets are [4, 17] , the first string occupies bytes 0..4 , and the second occupies 4..17 . This is a nice encoding because it lets us find a value without scanning everything before it, while still keeping the data packed together. Other options (e.g. from the Java impl) were to store a pair of shorts for each string - (start, length) . It allowed us not to check the previous entry to locate string j , but it used more space. Decisions decisions. NULL and empty strings both contribute zero bytes to the string data section; the bitmap determines which one it is. Example For a schema like this: id int name string age int email string and a row like: { id = 1, name = "Mary", age = 25, email = "mary@mail.com" } we have two integer columns and two string columns. Mary uses 4 bytes and mary@mail.com uses 13 bytes, so the row total is: 6 + 8 + 8 + 4 + 17 = 43 bytes The row is laid out like this: row-relative range contents 0..6 header: 43, 2, 2 6..14 integers: 1, 25 14..22 bitmap: 0 22..26 string end offsets: 4, 17 26..43 blob: "Mary" followed by "mary@mail.com" The actual bytes are: 2B 00 02 00 02 00 header 01 00 00 00 19 00 00 00 integers 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 bitmap 04 00 11 00 string end offsets 4D 61 72 79 "Mary" 6D 61 72 79 40 6D 61 69 6C 2E 63 6F 6D "mary@mail.com" Why and how The implementation is pretty simple - just some public free floating functions. I kinda like the fact that I can do these - in Java I had to have a static class for these methods. Anyways, nothing special - just a function that receives a row & schema and produces a binary array if validation passes. Another one that does the opposite. Schemas are always passed for double checking. Rows by themselves, while they can be read and decoded, do not contain schema information (like column names or anything like that). It's pretty much the same design as I had in Java, with the NULL bitmap added - it worked pretty well there. AI in the repo When I started this project I decided the limit the amount of AI I use - not cause I have anything against it, but because the goal of this project is for me to learn stuff and think things through, so having an agent write the implementation for me would have deprived me of those lessons - topic for another day, but I don't think you can actually learn something by having an AI do it. Anyways, the other goal for the project was to do it more 'correctly', as part of the lessons learned from the Java attempt. Some of the top items on this list are: do proper testing and have proper documentation. And I still stand by those decisions - they will definitely help down the line. But this is also a pet project, done in my (more often than not) limited time. And it turns out that not only do they use a lot of time when there is only one person who has to handle them, but they also leave one quite tired. Perhaps that's one of the reasons I've not worked as much on this lately - whenever I opened the project, I was presented with the docs I had been working on previously, still in a draft state, still a long way to go. Or I would look at the method I had just written and realize I would need to spend at least an hour testing it and validating everything. Useful, but boring. So this weekend I've spent some time designing some agent skills to help me with that. The goal is still not to have AI write the code - but the help with the repetitive and uninteresting maintenance tasks, so I can write the code myself. Skills Maintenance Started with some skills that handle technical docs - look at what's already there, what's implemented and keep the docs up to date. On demand or scheduled, depending on the situation. Also added some reviewer-style skills: mostly looking for gaps in docs, tests, reviewing any drifts in architecture, dependencies, tech debt, etc. One can be executed pre-PR: it checks the docs, checks the tests, does a review of the code changes to identify any obvious issues. Nothing fancy. Requirements and testing Coming from the regulated field of medical software, I also thought I could apply some of the things from that way of working (simplifying things by making them more complex, I know.) Namely, one area that I knew from the beginning I would need, but did not feel like doing was requirements. And once you have those, testing becomes a bit easier (so does implementing). So as a next step, I implemented a few other skills with the following goals: turning rough ideas into precise requirements proposing test cases from those requirements reviewing for gaps in the test design implementing approved tests without drifting into implementation guessing The workflow is based on the following skills: requirements-engineer grills me about one topic/area (based on docs/what I give as input/domain knowledge) and proposes requirements for the desired implementation, stored in docs/reqs.md blackbox-test-designer produces tests from the requirements without reading the production implementation whitebox-test-designer looks at the code and proposes edge-case and unhappier flow scenarios test-implementer turns the approved cases into Rust tests None of them run automatically and the transition from each step to the next requires my review & approval. I did a small trial run on the Schema component, and it was relatively useful. The grill-me part was probably the most useful and tbh I think the one that will be the most valuable in the future - partially cause it does write the reqs for me, but also cause it forces me to think of various edge cases, flows and other things I might have missed. The reqs it produced were ok - I had to do some tuning, but in the end they were ok. The test cases were also relatively ok - I had to tame it down since it ended up doing way too many for such a simple thing. The test cases implementation - I left this one sorta open in the skill, so that depending on the situation I can decide whether I want it to implement them as unit tests, public API tests, fully functional tests. This also does not mean I won't write any more tests or at least provide test cases, but I'll the the agent handle the large chunk of it - while I still think that they are important, a big chunk of them are relatively mechanic, throwing multiple inputs and checking the outputs. Also writing tests that verify the correct bytes are placed in the correct places in an array is not a super fun experience for me, not matter what. Haven't had the chance yet to determine if these will be useful or not, we'll have to see. During the following weeks I'll continue both with the implementation of new features and with some regression improvements - updating docs for existing functionality, adding requirements & tests. For as long as I still have credits in Codex I guess.

title: AI Search Can't See Your Site? The 5-Minute robots.txt Check
author: MEER
summary: Originally published on DigiHustle . Something odd is happening on the web right now. AI assistants answer more shopping and research questions every month, but websites are blocking the bots that feed those answers at a record pace. New numbers tell the story. Sites on Cloudflare's network denied 13.47% of AI bot requests in the third quarter of 2026, up from 5.98% a year earlier, according to Cloudflare Radar data analyzed by TechnologyChecker.io and reported October 9. A separate snapshot of 4,242 robots.txt files found sites block GPTBot 1.6 times for every site that allows it. Meanwhile the crawlers keep knocking: search-triggered AI crawl requests nearly doubled from 6.51% of AI crawl activity in Q2 to 11.92% in Q3. Read that twice. AI systems want to read your site more than ever. Site owners are saying no more than ever. Somewhere in the middle, businesses are becoming invisible to AI search without realizing it. Most blocks are accidents, not strategy Here's the uncomfortable part: in our experience, most sites blocking AI crawlers never made that decision on purpose. It usually goes like this. Someone enables Cloudflare's one-click "block AI bots" toggle during setup and forgets it exists. A WordPress security plugin ships with aggressive bot rules and the owner never reviews them. A developer copies a robots.txt template from a forum post in 2024 that disallows every bot it can name. A store gets hammered by scrapers one weekend, blocks everything in a panic, and nobody reverts it on Monday. We've seen the panic version more than once. A site under a scraping attack turns on every protection available, the attack stops, and six months later the owner wonders why ChatGPT never mentions their brand while competitors show up in every answer. The block did its job. Then it kept doing its job long after the threat left. That's the pattern to watch for: a temporary defense that quietly becomes a permanent handicap. The check takes five minutes You don't need an audit or a consultant for this. Open a browser and go to yoursite.com/robots.txt. Read it like a bouncer's guest list. Look for lines naming these crawlers: GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, Bytespider. If you see Disallow: / next to any of them, that crawler is turned away at the door. A blanket User-agent: * followed by Disallow: / blocks everyone, AI or otherwise — and yes, we still see live business sites running exactly that. Second, check your CDN or firewall. This is the step most guides skip, and it matters: a firewall or bot-protection rule can return a 403 denial even when robots.txt allows the crawler. In Cloudflare, that's Security → Bots. In other setups, it's whatever managed bot protection your host enabled. If server logs are available, search them for GPTBot or PerplexityBot entries and look at the response codes. A wall of 403s next to crawler user-agents is your answer. Third, don't trust a single tool's verdict blindly. Free robots.txt testers sometimes cache old versions of the file. Fetch the live file yourself. It takes thirty seconds and it's the ground truth. Which bots to let in (our take) Not every crawler deserves access, and anyone telling you to allow everything is selling something. Here's how we'd draw the line. Allow the crawlers behind assistants that cite sources and send traffic: GPTBot and OAI-SearchBot (ChatGPT), ClaudeBot (Claude), PerplexityBot (Perplexity). These are the bots that read your pages so an assistant can quote you. When someone asks "what's the best budget espresso grinder," the assistant can only recommend a product page it was allowed to read. Be more cautious with pure training crawlers like Google-Extended and Bytespider if bandwidth costs worry you — they feed model training, not direct citations. That's a legitimate business call either way. What isn't legitimate is blocking everything by default out of vague unease. That's the digital equivalent of locking your shop because window shoppers annoy you. You're not stopping theft; you're stopping customers. One more thing people get wrong: blocking AI crawlers doesn't meaningfully protect your content from being used in training anyway. Your pages are already in Common Crawl and a dozen other datasets. The block mostly costs you visibility in answers, not privacy. What invisibility actually costs This isn't abstract. We recently wrote about getting your store ready for AI shopping agents — structured product data, clear pricing, fast pages. All of that preparation is worthless if the agent's crawler bounces off your robots.txt. The agent can't recommend what it can't read, and it will recommend a competitor's product instead. That's not a theory; it's how retrieval works. The direction is one-way. Rank Math predicts AI visibility becomes a standard SEO metric in 2027. Rezolve AI's October announcements cited a McKinsey estimate of $3 trillion to $5 trillion in agent-mediated commerce by 2030. Every quarter you spend invisible is a quarter where competitors' pages become the default answers and yours don't exist. And once your crawler access is fixed, what the bots find matters too. Product descriptions written to convert pull double duty now — they sell to humans and they're the exact text AI assistants quote back. Thin, duplicated manufacturer descriptions give assistants nothing to cite. The honest caveat Allowing crawlers doesn't guarantee AI assistants will cite you. They won't. Assistants cite a handful of sources per answer, they favor pages that directly answer the question, and nobody outside the labs knows the full ranking recipe. Fixing robots.txt moves you from "impossible" to "possible," which is a big move, but it's the start of the work, not the end. Also, keep the data in perspective: the 13.47% figure covers Cloudflare's network only, and TechnologyChecker.io labels the Q3 numbers preliminary. Your site's reality could be better or worse. That's exactly why you check your own logs instead of trusting an industry average. Different assistants also run different crawlers, so "allow AI bots" isn't one switch. ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude each handle crawling differently , which means a robots.txt that welcomes one assistant can still shut out another. Check the names, not just the concept. Do it today Open your robots.txt. It takes less time than reading this article did. If you find AI crawlers on the block list and you didn't put them there deliberately, that's a five-minute fix for a problem that's been compounding for months. The web is splitting into sites AI can read and sites it can't. Make sure you're in the first group on purpose, not the second one by accident.

title: Designing an AI calling workflow: triggers, retries and recorded outcomes
author: Umashree H A
summary: Originally published as a Fonix.AI practical guide by AntEngage. This republication uses the same guide content. An answered call is only the beginning AI calling software answers or places telephone calls, understands the caller's request and helps execute a defined business workflow. To be useful, it needs more than a convincing voice: it must retrieve the right information, record the outcome and hand over to a person when the request goes beyond its scope. For an Indian business, a practical starting point is inbound enquiries or follow-up with people who requested contact. The goal might be a qualified enquiry, a confirmed callback or a booked appointment. Choose one of those outcomes before choosing a script, a call volume or a software plan. Fonix.AI by AntEngage runs voice agents, chat and campaigns in one platform, supporting 14+ Indian languages and cloud or on-premise deployment. This guide explains the workflow to evaluate with the team. Specific telephony, CRM and booking integrations should be confirmed against your existing systems before rollout. Choose the job before the calling tool A dialler, a voice broadcast and a conversational agent solve different problems. Start with what the recipient needs to do, not with how many calls the system can initiate. Tool What it does A sensible use Dialler Connects a call to a person or queue Staff conduct the conversation and decide the action Voice broadcast Delivers a recorded message An announcement does not require a conversation IVR Routes the caller through configured choices A small, predictable set of destinations Conversational voice agent Handles free-form replies within a defined workflow An enquiry needs clarification, a lookup, a booking or a handoff If a contact only needs a short announcement, an interactive agent may add unnecessary cost. If the recipient needs to ask a question or change a booking, a one-way recording will not finish the job. Evaluate both the normal path and the requests you expect to escalate. Connect the enquiry to a completed next step 1. Start from a trustworthy record An inbound call starts with the caller's request. Outbound follow-up should start from an enquiry or another agreed contact reason, with the appropriate permission, number and current status. Identify the system that owns this information and keep it current. Before an outbound attempt, check whether the person has already been contacted, opted out or completed the task. A fresh campaign upload should not erase those facts. Agree who maintains contact rules and how updates reach the calling workflow. 2. Define one useful conversation Write down the agent's job in a sentence: establish the enquiry, ask the agreed qualification questions, then arrange a callback with the right team. Give it the information it can use and the decisions it is allowed to make. Separate known facts from generated language. Course fees, appointment availability, property inventory and payment status must come from an approved source. When a fact is unavailable, the next action is clarification or handoff, not a plausible guess. 3. Handle the caller's language and timing Introduce the assistant clearly and establish whether it is a suitable time to talk. Let the caller change language, ask for a callback or request a person. A Hindi opening with English dates and regional place names is a realistic evaluation case. Fonix supports Indian-language and code-switched speech. Test with your own names, vocabulary and accents, including pauses, interruptions and corrected answers. A polished sample call does not establish how every call in your campaign will behave. 4. Read, confirm, act Retrieve information from the agreed system, confirm the caller's choice and then perform the permitted action. Announce a booked meeting or appointment only after the destination system confirms the write. If the write fails, retain an explicit pending outcome and offer the agreed alternative. For a callback, establish who will receive it and what time can genuinely be offered. For lead qualification, capture the useful answers and hand them to the appropriate team. Do not turn an uncertain answer into a stronger sales signal merely to improve a dashboard metric. 5. Finish with a usable outcome Store the request, relevant answers, agreed next step, action result and handoff reason. A transcript is useful evidence, but it is not a substitute for a record that tells the team what to do next. Use explicit statuses such as callback requested, booking confirmed, handoff pending, not interested or unresolved. These are illustrative categories, not a published Fonix API contract. Agree how they map into your actual CRM and which person owns each pending task. A follow-up example with an honest handoff This is an illustrative enquiry call, not a customer recording or a conversion claim. Assume a prospect has requested contact about a product demonstration. Assistant: नमस्ते, मैं आपकी demo enquiry के बारे में automated assistant बोल रहा हूँ। क्या अभी दो मिनट बात कर सकते हैं? Caller: अभी नहीं, कल afternoon call करना. Assistant: ठीक है। आपकी preferred language Hindi है या English? मैं callback request में दोनों details जोड़ दूँगा. Caller: Hindi. कल तीन बजे के बाद. Assistant: मैंने Hindi में, कल तीन बजे के बाद callback की preference note की है। हमारी team availability confirm करेगी। The assistant records a requested time, not a guaranteed appointment. If the workflow can retrieve a real team slot and reserve it, it can instead confirm the booking after a successful response. The wording follows the action result. A useful handoff tells the receiving team the enquiry source, preferred language, requested callback window, relevant qualification answers and any unresolved question. Send only information needed for the task through the configured system. Assign responsibility so the handoff does not end in an unattended queue. Build retries around state, not repetition Failure or interruption Workflow response What to verify Call is unanswered Apply the agreed attempt policy Attempts stop at the configured limit Caller requests a later call Record the preference and check scheduling rules The request is not treated as a completed sale Caller opts out Update the suppression source Later imports do not reintroduce the contact CRM is unavailable Keep an explicit pending state and an owner An update is not reported as saved when it failed Action times out Reconcile the destination record before retrying A retry cannot create a duplicate booking Caller disputes a fact Retrieve the approved record or escalate The agent does not invent an explanation Caller wants a person Transfer or assign a callback The receiving team has context and responsibility For write actions, agree how duplicate requests are detected. A request identifier or another supported reconciliation mechanism can distinguish a retry from a new task. Demonstrate the actual integration's behaviour; do not assume that a timeout means the first write failed. Pilot the system with failed lookups, interruptions and contradictory answers. If every test ends in success, you have not tested the operational boundaries. Figure 01. No answer, unknown result and completed task need different paths. Check integrations and deployment responsibilities Connection Questions to resolve before rollout Business number and telephony Which number is used, how are calls routed and what is the fallback? CRM or enquiry source Which fields can be read and updated, and how quickly do changes propagate? Calendar or booking system Can the integration reserve a slot, detect a conflict and reconcile a timeout? Confirmation channel What triggers a message, what is its delivery status and where are failures recorded? Human team Who accepts transfers and callbacks, and what happens outside staffed hours? Reporting Can the team trace an outcome back to its call and destination record? Fonix.AI can be deployed in the cloud or on-premise. Evaluate the complete system boundary: voice processing, telephony, integrations, records, staff access and ongoing maintenance. An on-premise model does not, by itself, make every connected service local. Ask the team to confirm available integrations and show the exact deployment you need. Assign owners for scripts, approved knowledge, contact policy, support and source-system changes. These responsibilities continue after the first live call. Compare cost per outcome, not just per minute A per-minute quote is an input to the budget, not the final cost of the workflow. Ask what is included: platform access, business numbers, telephony, connected or attempted minutes, setup, integration work, support and recording storage where relevant. Use a worksheet with your own expected volumes. Do not apply one estimate to both answered calls and unanswered attempts without checking how they are billed. Budget input What to establish Connected call minutes Expected answered calls multiplied by their average connected duration Other billed attempts The provider's billing rules for unanswered, failed and partial calls Fixed charges Platform, numbers and any agreed recurring support One-time work Setup and integration costs, with a clear scope Human handling Time spent on transfers, exceptions and callbacks Completed outcomes Verified bookings, qualified handoffs or completed callbacks For the same reporting period, divide the total included operating cost by the number of verified completed outcomes. State what the total includes and keep quality measures beside the calculation. A low cost per outcome is not useful if the booking is wrong or the callback never happens. Review current Fonix pricing and ask for estimates at both pilot volume and expected operating volume. Cloud and on-premise deployments have different cost structures; request a scoped quote rather than infer one from a generic rate. Figure 02. Total operating cost ÷ verified completed tasks = cost per outcome. An evaluation checklist for the live demo Bring one real workflow, a sample record without sensitive customer data, preferred languages and the actions the team needs to complete. Ask the demo to show: A normal enquiry with a verified next step. A language change and an interruption halfway through the call. A source-system lookup that fails. An action whose response is delayed or uncertain. A request for a human and a callback outside staffed hours. An opt-out followed by another attempt or import. The final outcome record and the person responsible for any pending work. Compare the evidence against the work your staff currently do. Launch one bounded workflow, review the unresolved outcomes with the team and expand only when the records and handoffs are reliable. Questions buyers ask about AI calling software Is an AI calling agent the same as a dialler? No. A dialler connects calls; an agent conducts a defined conversation and may retrieve information or trigger actions through configured integrations. Choose based on the task, not the label. Can it connect to our existing CRM? Discuss the CRM, access requirements and fields your workflow needs with the Fonix team. An integration must support the specific reads, writes and failure handling required. Do not assume every CRM is available as a ready-made connector. Can it make calls in Hindi and regional languages? Fonix supports 14+ Indian languages and code-switching. Evaluate your particular language mix and business vocabulary in a real call. The platform overview explains the broader voice, chat and campaign capabilities. What should stay with a person? Requests outside the approved workflow, disputed facts, sensitive judgement and any explicit request for a human need a defined handoff. Agree that boundary before running a campaign. Evaluate your own calling workflow Ask the Fonix team to review your workflow . Bring the enquiry source, language requirements, expected volume and one action you want the call to complete. Ask for an integration walkthrough and a demonstration of both success and failure. Explore the Fonix platform , the clinic receptionist workflow and current pricing as you compare your options.

title: GPT-6's Intelligent UI: The Business Tasks We'd Actually Trust It With
author: MEER
summary: Originally published on DigiHustle . ChatGPT Stopped Answering Questions and Started Building Tools On October 7, OpenAI rolled out GPT-6 with something it calls Intelligent UI. The short version: ChatGPT can now generate interactive interfaces inside the chat — calculators, bill splitters, comparison charts, adjustable diagrams, checklists — instead of just text. Paid users (Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise) got it first with a model called GPT-6 Sol. Free and Go users were scheduled to get GPT-6 Luna from October 8. The mechanism is what makes it interesting. OpenAI built a library of native, streamable components plus a compiler that assembles the interface while the model is still generating its answer. Parts of the UI appear before the full response finishes. OpenAI also claims GPT-6 Instant starts responding 44% sooner than GPT-5.6 Instant on questions that need web search. That's OpenAI's own internal testing — nobody outside the company has verified it yet, and you should read it that way. We spent the week feeding it the kind of small jobs that usually mean opening another tab, signing up for a free trial, or bothering a developer. Here's what happened. What We Actually Asked It to Build We gave it five unglamorous business tasks: Split a $340 team dinner bill four ways, with one person skipping alcohol and a 20% tip. Build a savings calculator for a freelancer setting aside 25% of irregular monthly income. Turn a messy pros-and-cons list of two email tools into a side-by-side comparison chart. Make an interactive checklist for onboarding a new client. Explain a loan amortization schedule with adjustable inputs. Tasks 1, 3, and 4 came out genuinely useful. The bill splitter let us drag the tip percentage and toggle the non-drinker, and every number updated live. That is the whole point of the feature — the interface fits the question, instead of you reading an answer and re-typing it into a separate calculator. Task 2 looked great and hid an assumption: it used a flat monthly income even though we'd described an irregular one. Task 5 was the one that made us pause. The schedule was immaculate. Clean sliders, tidy columns. And one of the interest totals was wrong. The Part Nobody's Talking About: Pretty Math Is Still Math You Didn't Check This is the mistake we see most often with new AI features, and Intelligent UI makes it worse. A generated calculator with crisp sliders and a confident layout makes an unsupported assumption look authoritative. OpenAI's own launch notes admit the model's design judgment still needs work — and that an interactive response "can also be incorrect." The bad practice to kill immediately: copying a generated number into a client invoice, a budget, or a loan document without re-running the math yourself. We now treat every Intelligent UI number the way we treat a junior analyst's spreadsheet — useful, fast, and guilty until verified. Cross-check with one independent calculation. When the number involves money, legal exposure, or health, that's non-negotiable. Three Small Subscriptions This Quietly Replaces Here is our strong opinion: if you're paying for a standalone widget tool that does one simple interactive thing — a mortgage calculator embed, a quote estimator, a quiz builder — GPT-6's Intelligent UI probably covers 80% of it for free inside a chat you already pay for. We cancelled a $19/month calculator widget subscription the same week we tested this, because the in-chat version handled every use case our team actually had. Our free AI tools roundup just got quieter too — this feature makes half of those "free tier" entries redundant. The 20% it doesn't cover: anything you need to publish, embed on your site, or hand to a customer. Intelligent UI lives inside your chat. OpenAI hasn't described any way to export one of these interfaces as a standalone app you can share. If your visitors need to use the tool, you still need real software. What It Can't Do Yet (the Honest List) No Pro reasoning mode — that still runs on GPT-6 Astra, which doesn't support Intelligent UI. Not in ChatGPT Work, Codex, or Voice. This release changes the Chat tab only. The older macOS and Windows desktop apps don't support it. OpenAI tells those users to switch to the web. You can reduce the visuals in settings ("Layout and visuals"), but you can't get a pure text-only mode — and you can't force an interactive answer for every prompt either. The model decides. The Free-tier rollout was announced for October 8, but OpenAI's own help page has shown conflicting status since. Check your model picker instead of assuming you have access. That last point deserves a second look. We're not sure yet whether the Free rollout is finished or still staggered by region and account type. If no interface appears for you, it's almost certainly the rollout, not your prompting. Getting the Good Interfaces Instead of Text Walls The model decides whether a question deserves an interface, so prompt shape matters more than usual. What worked for us: Ask for the tool, not the answer. "Build me a bill splitter for..." beat "How do I split a bill?" every time. Name the inputs explicitly — the amounts, the percentages, the variables you want to adjust. One task per message. Compound requests came back as text; focused ones came back as widgets. This is the same selection logic we lay out in our guide to picking the right AI app for your workflow : match the tool to the job instead of forcing one app to do everything. The Verdict: A Free Intern, Not a Developer Intelligent UI is genuinely useful and genuinely unfinished. For quick, disposable, one-person tools — the stuff you'd previously do in a spreadsheet or a free web widget — it's already good enough to replace paid micro-tools. For anything customer-facing, shared with a team, or where a wrong number costs real money, it's a drafting assistant, not a replacement. One honest caveat: we have not independently verified OpenAI's 44%-faster claim, and a week of testing is not a durability test. Interfaces that impress on day one can develop quirks by day thirty. We'll revisit this in a month and update the post — and when rival assistants ship their own generated interfaces, our ChatGPT vs. Gemini vs. Claude comparison is getting a full rewrite. For now: use it for the small stuff, verify every number that matters, and stop paying for widgets a chat window builds for free.
